statement:
Acts of Intelligence brings together 100 works from connected cultural collections to trace a longer history of agency: objects that see, measure, store, move, calculate, perform and appear to answer back.

This is not a narrow history of artificial intelligence. It is a cultural prehistory of agents. A telescope extends sight. An anatomical plate turns the body into a readable system. A praxinoscope, telephone, game, aircraft or control room delegates memory, judgement and action to a thing.

Every object can be opened and questioned through AUXIO. The replies are grounded in the object record, with the source institution, rights state and curatorial link kept visible.

sections.title: Seeing and Measuring
sections.intro: Instruments, images and systems that make the world observable. These works frame intelligence as a way of looking, measuring and converting distance into knowledge.
sections.question: What happens when an object teaches us how to see?

works.title: Camera
works.description: Camera. Camera. Made by Standard Camera Ltd.. Photography Centre, Room 108
works.curatorial_link: Nestled among early optical devices, this camera from the late 19th century represents a pivotal moment when photography transitioned from cumbersome processes to more accessible technologies. Manufactured by Standard Camera Ltd., it embodies the era’s leap towards mechanized vision, transforming how we capture and interpret the world around us. As part of 'Seeing and Measuring', this object underscores the camera’s role in extending human perception, turning visual experiences into quantifiable data that fuels our understanding of intelligence beyond the biological realm.

works.title: Rolleiflex camera and case owned by William Houston Rogers
works.description: Rolleiflex camera and case owned by William Houston Rogers. Camera. Made by Rollei. ca. 1955. Made in Germany. In Store
works.curatorial_link: Step into the world of precision and perception through a Rolleiflex camera from around 1955, crafted by Rollei in Germany. This iconic twin-lens reflex camera, with its sleek design and advanced features, epitomizes the era’s quest to capture reality with unparalleled accuracy. As part of 'Seeing and Measuring', it illustrates how instruments extend our visual capabilities, transforming observation into quantifiable data that fuels intellectual pursuits and artistic expression alike.

works.title: Radiograph of telephone handset
works.description: Radiograph of telephone handset. Radiograph of telephone handset. 1936. Prints & Drawings Study Room, level F
works.curatorial_link: Embedded within the intricate web of technological evolution, this radiograph from 1936 captures a telephone handset in X-ray precision, revealing the inner workings that extend beyond the visible spectrum. The image transforms the mundane object into a map of hidden mechanisms, illustrating how instruments like the telephone both extend our sensory reach and quantify the world around us as data points. This visualisation aligns with the exhibition’s exploration of artificial intelligence by highlighting the historical progression from extending human senses to machines that now interpret and generate complex patterns of information independently.

works.title: Folding camera used by Herbert Ponting
works.description: Folding camera used by Herbert Ponting. Camera. Made by A. E. Staley and Co. Made in London. In store
works.curatorial_link: Herbert Ponting’s folding camera, crafted by A. E. Staley and Co., transforms the act of seeing into a precise measurement of light and shadow. Employed by the intrepid photographer during his Antarctic expeditions, this instrument captures the raw beauty of the icy landscape, turning subjective visual experiences into objective data that can be analyzed and shared. As part of the 'Seeing and Measuring' section, it illustrates how technological advancements extend our sensory capabilities, enabling us to perceive and understand the world with unprecedented clarity and depth.

works.title: Sky Study, Paris
works.medium: albumen print from wet collodion negative
works.description: This view frames the city so that the dome of the chapel of Les Invalides—a retirement home and hospital for military veterans—dominates the skyline. In the 1850s, the light-sensitive coatings for photographic plates were incapable of properly exposing both earth and the sky in a single shot. Marville here set his camera to capture the dramatic sky and clouds, which meant that the city below, for the most part, became a dark mass of undifferentiated buildings. The scale, drama, and majesty of this natural spectacle overwhelm human achievements.
works.curatorial_link: Charles Marville's "Sky Study, Paris" from 1856–57, an albumen print made from wet collodion negatives, captures a moment when technology and artistic vision intersected. Framing the cityscape with the dome of Les Invalides chapel at its apex, Marville challenges conventional photographic techniques by prioritizing the dynamic sky over the earthly architecture below. The light-sensitive materials available during this period struggled to balance exposure between earth and heaven; thus, Marville's decision to highlight the dramatic clouds and celestial expanse reveals a sophisticated understanding of how instruments can extend human perception to measure and record atmospheric beauty with precision.

works.title: Astronomical Telescope (Gregorian reflector type)
works.institution: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa
works.description: This brass astronomical telescope is a Gregorian reflector type, made by Heath and Wing of London in about 1765. This type of telescope was invented by Scottish astronomer James Gregory in 1661. It uses two specially shaped metal mirrors to reflect light and create a magnified image, whereas earlier telescopes had used glass lenses to refract light. Gregory’s design resulted in smaller telescopes that produced sharper images, and was the forerunner of modern reflector telescopes. This telescope is associated with James Cook, an explorer who in 1768 was asked to command a long voyage to the Pacific to make astronomical observations. works.curatorial_link: Beneath the polished brass surface of this Gregorian reflector telescope lies a technological leap that transformed how we observe the cosmos. Constructed by Heath and Wing around 1765, it embodies James Gregory's innovative 1661 design, which utilized curved metal mirrors to reflect light and form magnified images. This shift from glass lenses reduced size and improved image quality, extending human vision into realms previously unobservable and turning the heavens into a measurable scientific domain.

By transforming geographical features into precise measurements and navigable lines, it extends human vision beyond immediate sensory perception, turning complex terrain into quantifiable data that informed military strategy and territorial claims. This object underscores how instruments and technologies have historically played a role in extending our understanding and control over the world around us, a theme central to the exploration of intelligence throughout this exhibition.

works.description: In December of 1968, the crew of Apollo 8 became the first people to leave our home planet and travel to another body in space. works.curatorial_link: On December 8, 2017, NASA released a stunning recreation of the iconic "Earthrise" photograph taken during the Apollo 8 mission in 1968. This image, reconstructed from data collected by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), captures Earth rising above the lunar horizon, a moment that not only extended human vision beyond our planet but also transformed our perception of home as a fragile oasis in space. In "Seeing and Measuring," this visual milestone illustrates how instruments can extend our senses to measure and interpret the cosmos, reflecting on the profound intelligence embedded in both human curiosity and technological innovation.

This image underscores how technology has long partnered with human intelligence to turn complex observations into precise measurements, essential for navigating the uncharted territories of space exploration.

sections.title: Bodies as Systems
sections.intro: Anatomy, gesture, sensation and repair. Long before AI, collections treated the body as something that could be read, modelled, trained and extended.
sections.question: Where does intelligence sit between body, image and tool?

By dissecting and diagramming the intricate web of muscles and tendons, artists and scientists like de Lairesse sought to unravel the secrets of bodily function, positioning human anatomy at the intersection of biology and mechanics.

sections.title: Instructions and Mechanisms
sections.intro: Machines, tools and devices that store instructions in matter. The room looks at agency as something designed into clocks, apparatus, craft and control systems.
sections.question: When does a mechanism begin to behave like an agent?

The sheer force required to rip apart a thick book filled with city-wide listings underscores not only the physical capabilities of human beings but also invites us to consider the mechanical and computational efforts needed to organize and distribute such information. In the context of 'Instructions and Mechanisms', this object highlights how early 20th-century technologies relied on intricate systems, much like the structured data in a telephone directory, which laid foundational principles for later developments in artificial intelligence.

As part of the 'Instructions and Mechanisms' section, it invites visitors to consider how mechanical systems for organizing data—like telephone directories—reflect human interaction with machines and challenge our perceptions of intelligence beyond mere computation.

works.curatorial_link: Charles-Émile Reynaud’s Praxinoscope Théâtre invites visitors to explore the early magic of animation through intricate mechanisms that transform static images into fluid motion. By allowing users to interchange various background plates and character discs, this interactive model demonstrates how encoded instructions can bring visual narratives to life, echoing the exhibition's broader narrative on artificial intelligence as a quest to mimic human thought processes through mechanical means.

As part of 'Instructions and Mechanisms', this object underscores how early civilizations encoded complex cultural narratives within mechanical devices, laying foundational concepts for machines that process information beyond simple automation.

works.title: Hawkins Machine Model F automatic stamp franking machine
works.description: This Hawkins automatic stamp franking machine was the latest technology in the late 1920s, employing a gas meter-like system for stamping and franking business mail quickly and efficiently. It followed on from Moss franking machines which were at the leading edge of postal technology in the early 20th century. New Zealand engineer Ernest Moss invented 'Moss Machine No. 1' in about 1904, followed quickly by a series of innovative machines until the mid-1920s when C.R. Hawkins took over. This particular machine only has two impressions (1d and 2d), and was manufactured by The Automatic Franking Machine Company which had been founded by Messrs Moss and Dombrain.
works.curatorial_link: Nestled within the evolution of automata and clockwork mechanisms lies the Hawkins Machine Model F automatic stamp franking machine, a testament to the ingenuity that defined early mechanical intelligence. This gas meter-inspired device revolutionized business mail processing by automating the task of stamping and franking with precision and speed during the late 1920s. As part of a lineage initiated by New Zealand engineer Ernest Moss's pioneering 'Moss Machine No. 1' in around 1904, this machine exemplifies how encoded instructions could transform mundane tasks into efficient, mechanized operations, illustrating the foundational principles that would later underpin artificial intelligence.

works.title: Printed Book of Hours (Use of Rome): fol. 95v, Text
works.artist: Guillaume Le Rouge (French, Paris, active 1493–1517); Master of the Très Petites Heures of Anne of Brittany…
works.description: Illustrated prayer books called books of hours remained popular with Europe’s elite well into the era of printing technology. This example belongs to a printed edition of five by the Parisian printer and engraver Guillaume Le Rouge, dating to 1510. Though printed on vellum (not paper), its 62 engraved pictures were hand-colored by an illuminator much like a traditional manuscript. By the mid-1480s, Paris was the center of production for books of hours with printed texts and engraved ornament. This book is therefore a hybrid fusing two distinct production methods—illumination and printing—representing the waning phase of the illuminator’s art prior to the complete transformation to printed books.
works.curatorial_link: Inscribed with intricate prayers and illuminated imagery, this printed Book of Hours from 1510 represents a pivotal moment where mechanical reproduction meets artistic craftsmanship. Created by Parisian printer Guillaume Le Rouge, it showcases how early printing technology began to democratize the production of religious texts while still preserving the bespoke beauty associated with hand-illuminated manuscripts. Each page, meticulously colored after engraving, bridges an era when human ingenuity was beginning to harness mechanical processes to animate and preserve sacred images and memories.

This work not only illustrates the early quest to animate the visual world but also highlights the intellectual challenge of replicating human and animal motion with mechanical precision—a precursor to modern artificial intelligence's pursuit of understanding and simulating cognitive functions.

works.title: Bwoom Mask
works.description: A mask from the Kuba Kingdom . Kuba mythology revolves around three figures, each represented by a masquerade character: Woot, the creator and founder of the ruling dynasty; Woot’s spouse; and Bwoom. Bwoom’s specific identity varies according to different versions of the myth. He may represent the king’s younger brother, a person of Twa descent, or a commoner. Embodying a subversive force within the royal court, the Bwoom masquerade is often performed in conflict with the masked figure representing Woot.
works.media_rights_basis: CC BY 3.0
works.curatorial_link: Bwoom Mask, originating from the Kuba Kingdom around 1900, embodies a subversive yet integral figure in Kuba mythology, whose identity fluctuates between representations of the king’s younger brother, an individual of Twa descent, or a commoner. works.title: Portrait of Eleanor Ramsay Fitzwilliam
works.artist: Charles Balthazar Julien Fevret de Saint-Mémin (French, 1770–1852)
works.medium: Black and white chalk on buff paper with pink wash in original frame
works.description: This portrait and its pair (2024.35.1), depict George Fitzwilliam, an English merchant, and his American wife Eleanor Ramsay Fitzwilliam, who sat in New York for the French émigré artist Charles Balthazar Julien Févret de Saint-Mémin. works.title: Red-Figure Column Krater (Mixing Vessel): Komos (Revel)
works.artist: Pig Painter (Greek, Attic, active c. 480–460 BCE)
works.description: Used for mixing wine and water at a symposium (drinking party), this vase bears images of komasts, or revelers, potentially mirroring the actions of its users. The three bearded men on side A stand out for their earrings, long drapery, and Eastern-style headdresses, and for the parasol held by one. Similar features have been noticed on numerous other red-figure vases, now called “Anakreontic” by scholars. This name refers to Anakreon, a 6th-century BC lyric poet from East Greece sometimes credited with inventing the barbitos, the long-stringed lyre played by the central figure on side A. The youths on side B, one draped, two nude and dancing, are less unusual.
works.curatorial_link: Inscribed with scenes of revelry from ancient Greek symposia, this red-figure column krater captures the essence of komasts—festive participants indulging in wine and song. The striking figures adorned with Eastern headdresses and parasols hint at the cultural exchanges that influenced Attic pottery during the late 5th century BCE. This vessel, crafted by the Pig Painter around 470–460 BCE, reflects the evolving image of artificial beings through its intricate human representations, challenging viewers to consider how ancient artisans envisioned and depicted intelligent social interactions.

works.title: Fragment from Black-Figure Neck-Amphora of Panathenaic Shape (Storage Vessel): Apollo and Zeus
works.artist: Antimenes Painter (Greek, Attic, active c. 530–510 BCE)
works.description: Comparison with better-preserved vases—and with other artworks and monuments, such as the famous Siphnian Treasury at Delphi—helps to fill in some of the action no longer surviving from the rest of this vase, which once showed Apollo and Herakles struggling for the Delphic tripod. One claw-footed leg of the tripod survives, across the chest of Zeus, the bearded figure who intervened to stop the quarrel between two of his sons. Apollo is the unbearded figure at left, while Herakles would have appeared beyond the break on the right.
works.curatorial_link: Amidst the intricate designs of this fragment from a Black-Figure Neck-Amphora by the Antimenes Painter, circa 520 BCE, a single claw-footed leg of a tripod emerges, telling part of a larger mythological struggle between Apollo and Herakles. This surviving element invites viewers to imagine the dynamic scene it once belonged to, where divine intervention halted the conflict. Such fragments offer glimpses into ancient narratives that explore competition among gods, reflecting early human fascination with intelligent, autonomous beings who interact in complex social spheres.

works.title: Black-Figure Lekythos (Oil Vessel): Pan Presenting Hare to Woman
works.artist: Asteas/Python Workshop (South Italian, Paestan, active c. 360–320 BCE)
works.description: This round-bodied oil vessel, produced in Paestum, belongs to a small group of vessels decorated with black figure in the second half of the fourth century BC, long after the technique had previously fallen out of fashion. Unlike most such vessels, which are smaller and feature just a single figure (often a woman or bird), this one shows a more complex and colorful scene. The goat-legged god Pan perches on a branched tree trunk, holding his syrinx (panpipe) and a hare. Facing him, her hands on the trunk, is a draped woman, perhaps a nymph or the moon goddess Selene.
works.curatorial_link: Amidst the rich tapestry of ancient Greek pottery, this black-figure lekythos from Paestum stands out for its intricate narrative. Crafted around 330–320 BCE by Asteas or the Python Workshop, it depicts the mischievous god Pan presenting a hare to a woman, a scene that brims with character and animation despite the stylized conventions of black-figure technique. This vessel challenges our perception of artificial beings, mirroring how ancient artisans imbued their static creations with life-like qualities, much like modern efforts to endow machines with intelligence and agency.

works.title: Bwoom Mask
works.description: A mask from the Kuba Kingdom . Kuba mythology revolves around three figures, each represented by a masquerade character: Woot, the creator and founder of the ruling dynasty; Woot’s spouse; and Bwoom. Bwoom’s specific identity varies according to different versions of the myth. He may represent the king’s younger brother, a person of Twa descent, or a commoner. Embodying a subversive force within the royal court, the Bwoom masquerade is often performed in conflict with the masked figure representing Woot.
works.curatorial_link: In Kuba mythology, the mask known as "Bwoom" embodies a complex and often subversive figure in the pantheon of masquerade characters, alongside Woot and his spouse. This intricate cultural object from around 1900 represents Bwoom, who can symbolize various identities within the community—ranging from the king’s brother to a commoner or someone of Twa descent. As part of the 'Faces of the Agent' section, this mask invites visitors to ponder how artificial beings in culture and technology similarly reflect our society's complex relationship with authority and identity.
